does-this-fuel-surcharge-match-the-contr.text:
← Freight accessorial invoice auditor

Does this fuel surcharge match the contract?

Fuel is billed as a percent of linehaul. The invoice often shows a dollar amount and no rate. A flat rate card skips FUEL because the base is the linehaul line, not a code. This page multiplies linehaul by the percent on the confirmation and compares that to the billed FSC line.

On the default $1,200.00 linehaul at 28%, the contract expects $336.00. A $412.00 billed line is 34.33% of linehaul — $76.00 above the contract. A typed bulletin of 26% plus 2 points is the same 28% and expects the same $336.00. Paste the confirmation percent. This page does not fetch DOE, EIA, or a carrier portal.

Path Percent of linehaul Amount vs billed

Complementary to the multi-line accessorial auditor (every billed extra), the detention clock, and who holds the cash after you pay the carrier. This page is only the fuel percent on one line. The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not claim the index you typed is the one the carrier used.

Common questions

Does this fuel surcharge match the contract?

Multiply linehaul by the contract fuel percent and compare that to the billed FSC line. On a $1,200.00 linehaul at 28%, the contract expects $336.00. A $412.00 billed line is 34.33% of linehaul — $76.00 above the contract. That is a review of the line, not a determination that the charge is wrong.

How do I check a fuel surcharge against the DOE or carrier bulletin?

Type the index percent from the bulletin you actually use and any points the contract adds. 26% plus 2 points is 28% and expects the same $336.00 on a $1,200.00 linehaul. The page does not fetch an index. Leave the index blank if the confirmation states a fixed percent.

how-to-audit-a-whole-freight-invoice.htm.text:
← Freight accessorial invoice auditor

How do I check a whole carrier invoice at once?

A partial review only ever finds what you already suspected. You open the invoice, look at the detention line that caught your eye, and never see the liftgate that was billed twice — because retyping every line into a spreadsheet is not worth an afternoon, so nobody does it.

The auditor now takes the carrier's own export. Load the file, confirm the columns, type your accessorial rates once, and the whole invoice is checked at once. The file is read inside your browser and never uploaded.

The four steps

  1. Export the invoice as CSV from the carrier portal or your TMS. A range copied out of a spreadsheet works too — paste it straight in, tabs and all.
  2. Check the guessed columns. Headings like Invoice Number, PRO Number, Charge Code, and Charge Amount are matched automatically, and every guess is shown in a dropdown you can correct.
  3. Type your rate card once — one CODE, amount per line, from the rate confirmation. This is the half the carrier's file cannot supply.
  4. Review what is flagged, then download the review CSV or copy the factual draft for the carrier.

A worked example

Six lines exported from a carrier portal:

Invoice Number,PRO Number,Charge Code,Charge Amount
INV-4471,PRO-77120,LINEHAUL,912.40
INV-4471,PRO-77120,FUEL,187.30
INV-4471,PRO-77120,LIFT,125.00
INV-4471,PRO-77120,LIFT,125.00
INV-4471,PRO-77120,DET,300.00
INV-4471,PRO-77120,RESI,45.00

…and a three-line rate card from the confirmation:

LIFT, 75
DET, 75
RESI, 45

With only import lines whose code is in my rate card ticked, line haul and fuel are skipped — and the page says so rather than quietly dropping them. That leaves 4 accessorial lines totalling $595.00, of which $325.00 is above the rate card across 3 flagged lines:

Line Billed Rate card Above Flag
LIFT$125.00$75.00$50.00Over expected
LIFT$125.00$75.00$50.00Over expected, possible duplicate
DET$300.00$75.00$225.00Over expected
RESI$45.00$45.00$0.00—

Those figures are recomputed from the same code the page runs, by a test that fails if this write-up and the tool ever disagree.

What it will not do

  • It does not invent an expected amount. A line whose code is not in your rate card imports with the expected column blank rather than copying the billed figure, which would make every line agree with itself and flag nothing.
  • It does not silently drop a line. An amount it cannot read — see attached, a blank cell — is imported as-is and flagged as an invalid billed amount. A dropped line in an audit reads as "nothing wrong here", which is worse than refusing to import it.
  • It does not pre-select an evidence status. Imported lines start at "not selected", because the file says nothing about what you can prove. Marking evidence is still yours to do, and it is what moves a line into the actionable count.
  • It does not decide anything. An overage against your typed rate card is a review finding, not a determination that a charge is wrong or a recommendation to withhold payment.

What a rate card looks like

Commas, spaces, colons, and equals signs all work, so a block pasted out of a confirmation usually needs no editing. Lines starting with # are ignored. A line that is not a code and an amount is reported back to you rather than skipped: 

# LTL accessorials, 2026 confirmation
LIFT, 75
DET 75
RESI: $45.00
LUMPER = 90

Rates that are not flat

Detention, storage, driver assist, and reweigh are rarely a single number. They are a rate per unit, usually past a free allowance and often under a cap — and they are the lines most worth checking, because the quantity is the part carriers and shippers disagree about. Write the rule the way the confirmation states it: 

DET 65/hr after 2 hours, max 325
STO $40 per day after 1 day
REWEIGH 4.50/cwt min 45
DRIVER ASSIST 35/hour, not to exceed 140
SORT 1.25/piece

Units understood are hour, minute, day, cwt, pallet, piece, mile, stop, and unit. Order does not matter: max 325 after 2 reads the same as after 2, max 325. The rate-card box reads every per-unit rule back to you in its own words, so you can see the allowance was understood as an allowance rather than folded into the rate.

A per-unit rule needs a quantity column mapped — hours, days, or weight. Map it in the same step where you map the amount column; headings like Detention Hours, Storage Days, and Billed Weight are guessed for you. If the quantity is in minutes and the rate is per hour, that one conversion is done and stated on the line. Any other mismatch — pallets against a per-hundredweight rate — is refused rather than guessed.

On a line billed $300.00 for detention with 5 hours on dock, against DET 65/hr after 2 hours, max 325, the expected amount is $195.00 and the line shows $105.00 above the rate card. The review queue, the CSV, and the dispute draft all carry the reason — 3 hours past 2 free × $65.00/hour — because a credit request that quotes the contract term is something the carrier's rating desk can check, and a bare expected figure is not.

If a per-unit code has no quantity, the line imports with the expected amount blank and the reason shown. It is never priced at zero: a $0.00 expectation would report the whole billed line as recoverable, which is a much more expensive kind of wrong than a gap you can see.

Complementary to the multi-line accessorial auditor (the review queue itself), the detention clock (one line against dock time), fuel percent versus linehaul, and who holds the cash (eat it, bill the customer, or review for a credit). This page is only about getting a whole invoice into the queue.

Common questions

How do I check a whole carrier invoice at once?

Export the invoice from the carrier portal or your TMS as CSV, load it into the auditor, confirm the guessed columns, and type your accessorial contract rates once as CODE, amount lines. Every imported line is then compared against your rate card. On a six-line example invoice, skipping line haul and fuel leaves four accessorial lines totalling $595.00, of which $325.00 is above the rate card — including a $125.00 liftgate billed twice.

Is my invoice uploaded anywhere?

No. The file is read inside your browser with the standard local file reader. There is no server, no account, no cookie, and no analytics vendor. Closing the tab discards everything you loaded.

What if my export does not say what I expected to pay?

It will not — a carrier invoice states what it billed, never what you expected. That is what the rate card is for: type each accessorial code and its contracted amount once and the importer applies it to every matching line. Lines whose code is not in your rate card still import and are still checked for duplicates, missing codes, and unreadable amounts.

How do I find a duplicate freight charge?

Import the whole invoice rather than the lines you already suspect. A line repeating the same invoice, reference, code, and amount is flagged as a possible duplicate, with no rate card needed. Double-billed accessorials are the finding a partial review misses, because nobody retypes the lines they are not already suspicious of.

index.html.text:
PRIVATE, LOCAL-FIRST AUDIT

Find freight accessorial overcharges before you pay.

Import the carrier's own invoice export, type your contract rates once — flat or per hour, day, or hundredweight with a free allowance and a cap — and get a review queue for duplicates, overages, missing codes, and missing evidence, each priced line saying which contract term produced its expected amount. Then copy a factual draft. Your rates price lines you type by hand the same way, so you can check a single detention charge without importing anything.

How do I check a whole carrier invoice at once? — import the export, apply your rate card, review what is flagged. Should I dispute this detention charge? — clock time after free time versus the billed detention line. Does this fuel surcharge match the contract? — linehaul times the confirmation percent versus the billed FSC line. Should I bill this accessorial to the customer? — eat it, invoice the customer, or pay first and file a review. This calculator vs. Trax Technologies — a local per-invoice check against an enterprise audit-and-payment platform. This calculator vs. Cass Information Systems — a local per-invoice check against a contracted freight audit and payment provider. This auditor vs. reviewing an invoice by eye — what a skim catches and what it misses.

Import the carrier's invoice

Nobody retypes a 200-line LTL invoice, and the duplicate you have not spotted is the one worth finding. Load the CSV your carrier portal or TMS exports — or paste the rows straight out of a spreadsheet. The file is read in this browser and never uploaded.

No invoice in front of you? — five accessorial lines carrying an overcharge, a duplicate, and a line that is billed correctly.

Which column is which?

Choose a file or paste rows and the columns are guessed from their headings. Check the guesses — an export that names its money column "Amount" cannot say what you expected, only what you were billed.

A carrier invoice states what it billed. It never states what you expected. Type the accessorial rates from your rate confirmation once and every imported line gets an expected amount to be checked against.

A rate can be flat (LIFT, 75) or per unit with a free allowance and a cap — DET 65/hr after 2 hours, max 325, STO $40 per day after 1, REWEIGH 4.50/cwt min 45. Per-unit rules need a quantity: map the column when you import, or type it in the Qty / hrs cell on a line you enter by hand. Units understood are hour, minute, day, cwt, pallet, piece, mile, stop, and unit. Your rates price both — leave a line's expected amount blank and the card fills it, showing which term it used.

No file loaded yet.

    Invoice lines

    One row per charge. Invoice and reference are optional labels. Billed and expected are dollars. Leave Expected blank and your rate card above prices the line — a greyed figure is the card's answer, and hovering it says which contract term produced it. Type your own figure to override it. Qty / hrs is only read by per-unit rules such as detention or storage.

    Invoice Reference Code Billed Qty / hrs Expected Evidence

    Review queue

    Above expected$0.00across entered lines
    Flagged0of 0 lines
    Actionable0overage plus missing or contradictory evidence

    Usage is optional, stays in this browser, and counts only audits, invoice imports, CSV downloads, and draft copies. Imported files are read locally and never uploaded — no invoice content, identifiers, cookies, or analytics service are used. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    Can I check a whole carrier invoice at once?

    Yes. Load the CSV your carrier portal or TMS exports, or paste the rows out of a spreadsheet. The columns are guessed from their headings and shown for you to correct. Type your accessorial contract rates once — one CODE, amount per line — and every imported line gets an expected amount to be checked against. On a six-line example invoice with line haul and fuel skipped, four accessorial lines totalling $595.00 import and $325.00 is above the rate card, including a liftgate billed twice. The file is read in your browser and never uploaded.

    How do I check detention or storage billed by the hour or day?

    Write the rule the way your confirmation states it — DET 65/hr after 2 hours, max 325 — and map the column holding hours or days. A line billed $300.00 with 5 hours on dock expects $195.00, so $105.00 is above the rate card, and the queue, CSV, and dispute draft all say why: 3 hours past 2 free at $65.00/hour. A per-unit code with no quantity imports with a blank expected amount and the reason shown, never a zero. Units understood are hour, minute, day, cwt, pallet, piece, mile, stop, and unit.

    How do I audit freight accessorial charges?

    Paste each billed line with the amount you expected from the rate confirmation, or leave the expected amount blank and let your rate card price it. The default demo is two $125 liftgate lines on INV-1 (expected $75, evidence missing), a $20 uncoded line that matches, and a $300 detention line with 5 hours on dock and no expected amount typed — the card rates it at $195.00, being 3 hours past 2 free at $65.00/hour. That is $205.00 above expected across 4 flagged of 4 lines, 3 actionable. The page flags duplicates, overages, missing codes, and invalid amounts. It does not decide whether to pay or dispute.

    Should I dispute this detention charge?

    Compare the billed detention line to the dock clock after free time. On 180 minutes on dock, 120 free, and $75/hour, 1.00 hour is billable — $75.00 expected. A $300.00 billed line is $225.00 above the clock, as if 4.00 hours. That is a review of the line, not a determination that the charge is wrong.

    On a prepaid collect shipment that already paid $180, a $300 detention against $75 supported leaves a $225.00 gap. Eating the line keeps −$120.00. Billing the customer $300.00 keeps $180.00. Paying first and getting that $225.00 credit after 1.5 hours at $42/hr ($63.00 labor) keeps $42.00. The same review with no credit keeps −$183.00. That is cash on these inputs, not a reason to invoice a customer or to file a claim.

    Does this fuel surcharge match the contract?

    Multiply linehaul by the contract fuel percent and compare that to the billed FSC line. On a $1,200.00 linehaul at 28%, the contract expects $336.00. A $412.00 billed line is 34.33% of linehaul — $76.00 above the contract. A typed bulletin of 26% plus 2 points is the same 28%. That is a review of the line, not a determination that the charge is wrong.

should-i-bill-this-accessorial-to-the-cu.text:
← Freight accessorial invoice auditor

Should I bill this accessorial to the customer?

Shippers search this after the carrier invoices detention, a liftgate, or a reweigh the quote never showed. AP can eat it, add a line on the customer invoice, or pay first and ask for a credit. Those are different cash.

On the default prepaid collect — $180.00 already collected, a $300.00 detention against $75.00 supported — the gap is $225.00. Eating the line keeps −$120.00. Billing the customer $300.00 keeps $180.00. A 1.5-hour review at $42/hr ($63.00 labor) that recovers the gap keeps $42.00. The same review with no credit keeps −$183.00.

The $225.00 gap buys 5.36 hours of review at that rate. A $50 gap against ten hours at $125/hr ($1,250.00) finishes $1,200.00 behind eating. Type the confirmation amount, not a portal default.

Path Customer pays extra Review labor Cash you keep vs eat

Complementary to the multi-line accessorial auditor, the detention clock, and fuel percent versus linehaul (is the bill right?). This page is who holds the cash after you pay the carrier. It does not invoice anyone or file a claim.

Common questions

Should I bill this accessorial to the customer?

On a prepaid collect shipment that already paid $180, a $300 detention against $75 supported leaves a $225.00 gap. Eating the line keeps −$120.00. Billing the customer $300.00 keeps $180.00. Paying first and getting that $225.00 credit after 1.5 hours at $42/hr ($63.00 labor) keeps $42.00. The same review with no credit keeps −$183.00. That is cash on these inputs, not a reason to invoice a customer or to file a claim.

When does reviewing a freight extra cost more than eating it?

When the gap is crumbs and the review is expensive. An $80 line against $30 supported is a $50 gap. Ten hours at $125/hr is $1,250.00 of labor. Eating that line on $80 already collected keeps $0.00. A credit still finishes $1,200.00 behind eating.

should-i-dispute-this-detention-charge.h.text:
← Freight accessorial invoice auditor

Should I dispute this detention charge?

Detention is billed as hours after free time. The invoice often shows a dollar amount and no clock. This page subtracts contracted free time from the minutes on dock, multiplies the remainder by the hourly rate on the confirmation, and compares that to the billed line.

On the default 180 minutes on dock, 120 free, and $75/hour, the clock leaves 1.00 billable hour — $75.00 expected. A $300.00 billed line is $225.00 above the clock, as if 4.00 hours. Paste your timestamps and the rate on the confirmation. This page does not fetch a carrier portal.

Measure Hours Amount

Complementary to the multi-line accessorial auditor (every billed extra), fuel percent versus linehaul, and who holds the cash after you pay the carrier. This page is only the detention clock on one line. The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not claim the timestamps you typed are the ones the carrier recorded.

Common questions

Should I dispute this detention charge?

Compare the billed detention line to the dock clock after free time. On 180 minutes on dock, 120 free, and $75/hour, 1.00 hour is billable — $75.00 expected. A $300.00 billed line is $225.00 above the clock, as if 4.00 hours. That is a review of the line, not a determination that the charge is wrong.

How is detention free time counted?

Billable hours are only the minutes after contracted free time. If the truck was on dock 180 minutes and free time is 120 minutes, 60 minutes — 1.00 hour — is billable at the contract hourly rate. The page does not decide whether the timestamps you typed are correct.

vs-cass.html.text:
← Freight Accessorial Invoice Auditor

This calculator vs. Cass Information Systems

Two different shapes: Cass Information Systems audits and pays freight invoices at scale across a shipper's whole carrier network, under an ongoing contracted relationship built for larger freight volumes. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — does this one carrier's invoice, checked line by line against your own contract rates, actually owe what it billed, before you pay it.

What each tool is for

Cass Information Systems (Nasdaq: CASS) is a publicly traded financial services company whose freight business, marketed as Cass Freight, provides freight audit and payment (FAP) processing to shippers: it receives carrier invoices — commonly by EDI or a direct feed from the shipper's TMS or ERP — audits each line against the shipper's contracted rates at scale, and disburses payment to the carrier on the shipper's behalf, alongside consolidated transportation spend data and reporting across the whole freight network. It is set up as an ongoing contracted relationship built for shippers with meaningful freight volume across many carriers and lanes: onboarding and integration, not a self-serve signup. Cass is also known for publishing the monthly Cass Freight Index, a widely cited industry benchmark of North American freight volumes and expenditures — a separate product from the audit-and-payment service itself. Cass's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, integrations, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not integrate with a TMS or ERP, ingest invoices by EDI, or pay a carrier. It takes one carrier's invoice — imported as a CSV export or pasted rows, or typed by hand line by line — maps its columns, and checks each accessorial line against a contract rate card you type once: flat amounts, or per-unit rules for hour, minute, day, cwt, pallet, piece, mile, or stop, each with its own free allowance and cap. It flags duplicate lines, amounts above the rate card, missing codes, and missing evidence, checks a detention charge against the dock clock and a fuel surcharge against the contracted percent of linehaul, and compares eating a line, billing it to the customer, or paying first and filing for a credit. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and the file you import is read locally and never uploaded.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a shipping operation with freight moving on many carriers and lanes, and want a contracted service to ingest invoices by EDI, audit them at scale, and pay the carrier.Cass Information Systems, or a comparable freight audit and payment provider.
I have one carrier's invoice — or one broker or small shipper's worth of them — and want to check it against my own contract rates right now, with no contract of my own to sign.This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
I need a detention or storage charge checked against free time and an hourly or daily rate, or a fuel surcharge checked against a contracted percent of linehaul.This calculator's detention-clock and fuel-surcharge checks.
I need my freight invoices actually paid to the carrier on my behalf, not just reviewed.Cass Information Systems, or a comparable FAP provider — this calculator has no payment feature at all.
Should I eat this accessorial line, bill it to the customer, or pay first and file for a credit?This calculator's cash-outcome comparison.
Do I need a contract, minimum volume, or an EDI integration to use the tool?This calculator: no. Cass and comparable FAP providers are sold as an ongoing contracted service.

Most freight-paying shippers get different value from each: Cass Information Systems (or a comparable freight audit and payment provider) for automated, at-scale invoice audit and carrier payment across a whole freight network under an ongoing contract, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check on one invoice or one accessorial line against contract rates before it is paid — including for a broker or small shipper whose freight volume would not clear a FAP provider's minimum. This page's own figures are a review of the lines you entered, not an audit run, a payment, or a determination that a charge is wrong.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Imported files are read locally and never uploaded.

vs-reviewing-an-invoice-by-eye.html.text:
← Freight Accessorial Invoice Auditor

Freight Accessorial Invoice Auditor vs. reviewing an invoice by eye

Reading a carrier invoice yourself catches the one line that looks obviously high. It reliably misses a second identical charge billed at an ordinary-looking price, the free-time-and-cap math behind a per-unit rate, a fuel surcharge never turned into a percent of linehaul, and whether an overage actually has evidence attached — which is what this free, no-upload auditor computes exactly, on every line.

Where reading it yourself stops being enough

Every AP clerk, broker, and small shipper who pays freight bills already does this: open the invoice, scan the lines, and flag whatever looks expensive. For the one line that is genuinely several times what a normal stop costs, that scan works — it is designed to catch exactly that. The problem is everything else on a real invoice does not look wrong on its own; it only becomes wrong when compared against something else, and a skim does not make that comparison.

What you're trying to catchReading the invoice yourselfThis auditor
One line that is obviously higher than a normal charge of that kind.Works. This is the case a scan is built to catch.Also catches it, in the same pass as everything below.
The same accessorial billed twice — same invoice, reference, code, and amount.Invisible on its own: an ordinary-looking price raises nothing, even read twice. Catching it means comparing every line against every other line, not judging one line at a time.Flagged automatically as a possible duplicate the moment two lines share invoice, reference, code, and amount.
A per-unit rate with a free allowance and a cap — detention, storage, reweigh, driver assist.Needs three steps in your head: subtract the free time, multiply the remainder by the rate, then check the cap. Easy to skip the subtraction when the total already looks plausible.Computed exactly, with the reasoning shown — e.g. "3 hours past 2 free × $65.00/hour" — not just a number.
Whether a fuel surcharge matches the contracted percent of linehaul.The dollar figure alone tells you nothing until it is divided by linehaul and compared to the contract percent — a division most reviews never actually run.Billed percent of linehaul computed and compared against both the contract percent and an optional index-plus-adder figure.
Whether a flagged overage actually has supporting evidence attached.Easy to lose track of which of several flagged lines you have a scale ticket or BOL for once the invoice runs past a handful of rows.Each line's evidence status is tracked against its own variance, so only an overage with missing or contradicting evidence counts as actionable.
The total dollar amount actually above the rate card across a whole invoice.Added up longhand, one line at a time — error-prone, and easy to double-count a line whose evidence already settled it.Totalled exactly, excluding lines that could not be priced and lines evidence already supports.

A scan for the one big line is still the fastest way to catch the charge that is obviously wrong, and this auditor is not doing anything a patient, line-by-line audit with a calculator and a highlighter could not — it is reading the same invoice a patient audit would, just comparing every line against every other line and against the rate card automatically instead of leaving those comparisons to be made by hand.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. An imported file is read locally and never uploaded.

Common questions

Can't I just review the invoice myself and catch the overcharges?

For one line that is obviously high -- a detention charge several times what a normal stop costs -- yes, that is often visible on a single read. What a read misses is a line repeated twice at an ordinary-looking price, a per-unit rate with a free allowance and a cap that needs a two-step calculation, a fuel surcharge whose percent of linehaul was never actually computed, and whether an overage has supporting evidence attached once the invoice runs past a handful of lines.

Why is a duplicate line harder to catch than one that looks expensive?

An expensive-looking line stands out on its own -- it triggers a "that seems like a lot" reaction independent of anything else on the invoice. A duplicate does the opposite: the second liftgate charge at the same ordinary price looks completely fine by itself, so reading it a second time raises nothing. Catching it means noticing that two separate lines share the same invoice, reference, code, and amount -- a comparison across rows, not a judgment about any one row -- which is exactly what a skim does not do.

What does the detention or fuel math actually require?

A per-unit accessorial like detention, storage, or reweigh is rarely a single number: it is a rate per hour or per hundredweight, usually past a free allowance and often under a cap. Getting the expected amount right means subtracting the free time first, multiplying only the remainder by the rate, then checking the cap -- three steps, and the middle one is easy to skip when a dollar figure already looks plausible. A contracted fuel surcharge is harder still to eyeball: the dollar amount alone says nothing until it is divided by the linehaul charge and compared against the contracted percent, which is a division most reviews never actually do.

If I already track evidence for each disputed line, doesn't that cover it?

Tracking whether you hold a scale ticket, BOL, or rate confirmation for each line is exactly the bookkeeping a real review needs -- but holding that alongside which lines are actually over the rate card, across an invoice with more than a handful of rows, is where a manual review loses the thread. An overage with supporting evidence attached is a settled line, not a dispute; an overage with no evidence, or evidence that contradicts the billed condition, is the one worth raising. Keeping that pairing straight by eye across a whole invoice is the same cross-row bookkeeping the duplicate check needs, one column over.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual review any shipper, broker, or AP clerk already does -- reading a carrier invoice and checking it against what they expect to owe. It names no competing product or company. The auditor makes no network request of any kind: everything runs in your browser, and an imported file is read locally and never uploaded.

Have a whole invoice to check at once? See how to audit a whole freight invoice, or open the Freight Accessorial Invoice Auditor directly.

This calculator vs. Trax Technologies

Two different shapes: Trax Technologies audits and pays freight invoices at scale across a shipper's whole carrier network, under an ongoing enterprise account. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — does this one carrier's invoice, checked line by line against your own contract rates, actually owe what it billed, before you pay it.

What each tool is for

Trax Technologies is enterprise transportation spend management (TSM) software, sold under an ongoing account to shippers with freight to audit and pay across many carriers and lanes. Its core freight audit and payment (FAP) service ingests carrier invoices — commonly through EDI and integration with a shipper's TMS or ERP — audits each line against the shipper's contracted rates at scale, and can disburse payment to the carrier on the shipper's behalf, alongside spend visibility and analytics reporting across the whole freight network. Setting it up is an enterprise engagement: onboarding, carrier and rate-card integration, and a contract, not a self-serve signup. Trax's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, integrations, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not integrate with a TMS or ERP, ingest invoices by EDI, or pay a carrier. It takes one carrier's invoice — imported as a CSV export or pasted rows, or typed by hand line by line — maps its columns, and checks each accessorial line against a contract rate card you type once: flat amounts, or per-unit rules for hour, minute, day, cwt, pallet, piece, mile, or stop, each with its own free allowance and cap. It flags duplicate lines, amounts above the rate card, missing codes, and missing evidence, checks a detention charge against the dock clock and a fuel surcharge against the contracted percent of linehaul, and compares eating a line, billing it to the customer, or paying first and filing for a credit. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and the file you import is read locally and never uploaded.
